rows.why: Item 7 asks what share applies when none is configured. With bounty 10000 and no share, the call recorded a hidden-tests release of 7500 and returned status 'partially released'. That is what S1 expects.

Item 2 asks how an uneven split is rounded. The pick rounds the hidden-test amount down using BigInt division and gives the remainder to UAT. splitBounty(101,7500) returned 75/26, which is rounded down and adds up to the bounty. BigInt keeps it exact up to MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, so 999 would give 749/250.

Item 12 asks what the UAT release amount is. The pick is the precomputed bounty minus the hidden-test amount. When the hidden-test share was actually released, as S3 assumes, that equals the remaining balance, and status becomes 'fully released'. The call returned 25 against a stored hidden release of 1, so it does not read a balance from the store. That only differs from S3 when the stored state is inconsistent, which S3 does not cover.

Item 8 asks what a failed hidden-test run does. The call returned {status:'locked', releases:[]} for the failure. The one write came from the pass handled after it, so the failure itself recorded nothing and the task stayed locked.
Item 1 asks what happens when UAT is approved before the hidden tests pass. The call threw 'the hidden tests have not passed, so the UAT release cannot be made' and made no writes (w: []).
Item 4 asks for the status and the release recorded on a zero bounty. The status is 'pro bono' as expected, but the call recorded {kind:'hidden-tests', amount:0}. S6 says no release is ever recorded.

Item 3 asks how a repeated event is handled, including the same kind with a new id. Any later event of a kind already released is a no-op whatever its id. In the call, a second hidden-tests-passed with a different id returned the saved state, and only one write was made.

Item 10 asks how concurrent and duplicate events are handled. Events go through a per-handler promise queue, so simultaneous calls run one after another, and the kind check from item 3 makes the second one a no-op. Two concurrent handles in the call gave the same state with one write in total.

Item 10 also covers store failures. In the call, the first set threw 'boom', the handle rejected with that error, and nothing was recorded. Handling the same event again then succeeded with exactly one write.
